answer:
### History of Music: Major Eras

Music history spans from early oral traditions through various structured periods of artistic and cultural development [SRC-9e80d2559b42].
Major historical eras include: [SRC-9e80d2559b42]

* **Medieval Music (500–1400):** Spanning the Middle Ages, this era was primarily religious and composed for the Catholic Church, famously characterized by single-line unison Gregorian chants [SRC-49178ada5e17].
* **Renaissance Music (1400–1600):** A period of artistic and cultural growth defined by polyphony, which involved multiple independent melodies played or sung simultaneously [SRC-49178ada5e17].
* **Baroque Music (1600–1750):** Marked by continued cultural expansion and characterized by ornate melodies [SRC-49178ada5e17].

### Great Musicians in History

Classical music history features many pioneers and geniuses [SRC-80ae72ad6448].
Widely recognized master composers include: (unverified: no matching retrieved evidence).

* **Johann Sebastian Bach (1685–1750):** Regarded as the definitive Baroque composer [SRC-80ae72ad6448], Bach was a prolific organist, violinist, and composer who pushed contemporaneous instruments to their limits across solo works, sacred choral pieces, and instrumental concertos like the *Brandenburg Concertos* [SRC-80ae72ad6448].
* **Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (1756–1791):** A child prodigy and defining figure of the Classical era [SRC-80ae72ad6448], Mozart composed 41 symphonies, numerous concertos, chamber works, and revolutionary Italian operas such as *The Marriage of Figaro* [SRC-80ae72ad6448].

Music History
Music isn’t just a subject to study; it’s a journey through history itself.
‍
Every piece of music is a chapter in a long, evolving story.
At La Maison, we don’t just teach notes and techniques; we connect you to the richness of music’s past.
We believe that each era has contributed to what music is today. From the simplicity of Gregorian chant to the complexity of Beethoven’s symphonies,
As you progress on your musical journey with us, remember that you’re not just playing notes. You’re weaving your thread into the vast, vibrant tapestry of music’s history, joining a community of artists who’ve been sharing this universal language across generations.
Keep reading to see this music history timeline.
Classical Music History Timeline
Medieval music (500-1400)
Medieval music is the music of the Middle Ages, which lasted from the 5th century to the 15th century. It was primarily religious music, and most compositions were written for the Catholic Church. The music of this period was characterized by Gregorian chant, which was a single-line melody sung in unison by a choir.
Renaissance music (1400-1600)
Renaissance music is the music of the Renaissance period, which lasted from the 14th century to the 17th century. It was a time of great artistic and cultural growth, and music was no exception. Renaissance music was characterized by polyphony, which was the use of multiple independent melodies played or sung at the same time.
Baroque music (1600-1750)
Baroque music is the music of the Baroque period, which lasted from the 17th century to the mid-18th century. It was a time of great artistic and cultural growth, and music was no exception. Baroque music was characterized by ornate melodies, complex harmonies, and elaborate instrumentation.
Galant music (1720-1770)
Galant music is a style of music that emerged in the mid-18th century. It was a reaction to the complexity of Baroque music and was characterized by a simpler, more elegant style. Galant music was characterized by simple melodies, light textures, and a focus on melody and harmony.
Classical period (1750-1820)
The Classical period is the period of music that followed the Baroque period and preceded the Romantic period. It was characterized by a focus on balance, clarity, and simplicity. Classical music was characterized by its use of simple melodies, clear harmonies, and elegant forms.
Romantic music (1780-1910)

Romantic music is the music of the Romantic period, which lasted from the late 18th century to the early 20th century. It was a time of great artistic and cultural growth, and music was no exception. Romantic music was characterized by its use of emotion, drama, and expression.

Picture:
PA / Getty
By Rosie Pentreath
@rosiepentreath
Introducing you to the most famous classical composers in music history, who have brought us the very best classical tunes ever written.
Classical music history is full of pioneers, practice-devotees and plenty of geniuses.
We’ve done our utmost, below, to distil these great men and women into a list of 30 of the very best.
These composers will give you the greatest introduction to classical music possible, so, without further ado…
Read more: The 15 most famous tunes in classical music
Johann Sebastian Bach (1685-1750)
Bach is the definitive Baroque composer. If you have sublime Bach you don’t need the others (and we’re only half kidding).
Born in 1685 in Eisenach in Germany, Bach was a prolific composer, organist , harpsichordist , violist, and violinist .
The music he wrote spanned forces – from solo instrumental works, such as the Cello Suites (below), to huge sacred choral pieces, instrumental concertos like the Brandenburg Concertos , and collections of keyboard music, including The Well-Tempered Clavier , that pushed contemporaneous instruments to their limits.
Read more: 10 of Bach’s all-time best pieces of music
See Me- A Global Concert - World Economic Forum
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (1756-1791)
Continuing the tradition of names with three words and four well-formed syllables in the middle one, is the child prodigy and all-round genius, Mozart .
Composing in, and defining, the Classical era, Mozart wrote 41 symphonies, numerous concertos, revolutionary Italian operas including The Marriage of Figaro and Cosí fan tutte , and chamber works that are loved as much by audiences today as when they were composed.
He had a tragically short life: after his incredibly successful career, Mozart sadly died at just 35 years old, leaving behind his profound, and profoundly beautiful, Requiem .
Read more: 10 life-changing pieces of music by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
Marriner at 90: Mozart Piano Concerto No. 20
Ludwig van Beethoven (1770-1827)
Beethoven ’s name is widely interchanged with the phrase ‘greatest composer who ever lived’. And we’re okay with that.
Beethoven, who composed in classical music’s Romantic era, absolutely revolutionised orchestral music with his Third ‘Eroica’ Symphony, writing music that captured the inner struggle of the individual alongside the sheer joy of life.
According to Beethoven expert and Classic FM presenter, John Suchet , “A good Beethoven performance should turn your knuckles white from gripping the arms of your seat, your nerves shredded, but leaving you imbued with a feeling of exhilaration and triumph — as well as deep love and admiration.” Yep.

Entry Overview
A concise timeline of Music, covering the major eras, breakthroughs, and turning points that shaped the field.
Intermediate Music
Music history is not a straight line from simplicity to sophistication. It is a long record of changing systems for organizing sound, storing memory, training performers, circulating repertories, and attaching music to ritual, power, entertainment, devotion, labor, and identity. A strong timeline has to keep both innovation and continuity in view. Readers should keep Music History: Main Topics, Key Debates, and Essential Background and Key Music Terms: Definitions Every Reader Should Know nearby, because historical turning points in music often make the most sense when changes in notation, instruments, listening habits, and institutions are read together.
Before Writing, Music Lived Through Memory, Ritual, and Transmission
Long before notation systems became stable, music moved through oral and embodied transmission. Songs, chants, drum patterns, dance forms, ceremonial calls, and instrumental practices were learned through repetition, imitation, and participation. This does not make early music primitive. It means its storage system was human rather than graphic. Memory, community, and ritual held the repertory together.
That early condition matters because oral transmission remained central even after writing emerged. Many traditions across the world continued to rely more on apprenticeship, participation, and localized practice than on notation. The later prestige of written music in some institutions should never be mistaken for the total history of music.
Ancient Civilizations Linked Music to Knowledge, Ceremony, and Order
In ancient Mesopotamia, Egypt, Greece, India, China, and other civilizations, music already carried theoretical, religious, and political significance. Instruments were built with care, court and temple musicians held recognized roles, and systems of pitch organization and ethical meaning were discussed in sophisticated ways. Ancient Greek writers, for example, connected music to mathematics, education, character, and civic order. South Asian traditions developed rich conceptual frameworks for melodic and rhythmic organization. Chinese thought often linked music to cosmic and political harmony.
The key breakthrough here was not one single invention but the recognition that music could be studied as an ordered practice. It was not only performed. It was theorized, classified, and tied to systems of knowledge.
Notation Changed Preservation Without Replacing Performance
